text: Classical convolutional neural networks revolutionized image classification by exploiting locality and weight-sharing. Quantum convolutional neural networks borrow the name and some structural ideas, but the analogy again needs careful handling rather than a straight transplant.

A classical CNN slides a filter across an image, reusing the same weights at every position, then reduces resolution with pooling. A QCNN, as proposed by Cong, Choi, and Lukin in 2019, redefines both ideas for qubits: a quantum convolution layer applies the same parameterized gate block to neighboring qubit pairs, and a quantum pooling layer measures a subset of qubits and conditionally acts on the rest, reducing the active qubit count.

This is the detail most often glossed over. Classical max-pooling keeps the most salient value from a local neighborhood, a clear, interpretable summary. Quantum pooling, by contrast, measures some qubits, an irreversible operation, and uses that outcome to decide what gate to apply to the rest. The analogy to classical pooling is structural, both reduce active degrees of freedom layer by layer, but the actual mechanism bears little resemblance.

The genuinely interesting, proven result behind QCNNs is specific: the original paper showed they can efficiently recognize certain quantum error-correcting code phases and quantum many-body phases of matter — a task about classifying quantum data, not classical images or spreadsheets. No application of a QCNN-style architecture has demonstrated a practical advantage over classical CNNs on classical data benchmarks.

Next lesson's lab traces a 2-qubit, 2-layer QNN-style circuit's forward pass entirely by hand, closing out this chapter by making the mechanics of entanglement and multi-qubit measurement fully concrete.
